text: Satkosia Tiger Reserve lies in central Odisha. It was declared a tiger reserve in 2007 by joining two older wildlife sanctuaries: the Satkosia Gorge Wildlife Sanctuary, created in 1976, and the Baisipalli Wildlife Sanctuary, notified in 1981. The reserve covers about 964 square kilometres, of which about 524 square kilometres is the core area. The reserve spreads across four districts of Odisha: Angul, Cuttack, Nayagarh and Boudh. Angul town is about 60 kilometres away from the reserve. The reserve is also part of the Mahanadi Elephant Reserve. The Satkosia Gorge and its name: The heart of the reserve is the Satkosia Gorge, where the Mahanadi River cuts through the hills of the Eastern Ghats. The gorge is about 22 kilometres long. The name Satkosia comes from "sat", meaning seven, and "kosh", an old unit of distance equal to about two miles. So Satkosia means a stretch of about seven kosh, or fourteen miles, which is the length of the gorge. Satkosia is special because two great natural regions meet here: the Deccan Peninsula and the Eastern Ghats. Because of this meeting, plants and animals of both regions are found together, which makes the area very rich in biodiversity. The Satkosia Gorge has also been recognised as a Ramsar site, which means it is a wetland of international importance.

section: Satkosia Tiger Reserve - Forests and plants
text: The forests of Satkosia are mainly mixed deciduous forests, with Sal trees as one of the most important species, along with riverine forests along the Mahanadi. More than 400 species of plants have been recorded in the reserve. Animals of Satkosia: Satkosia is home to many mammals, including the Asian elephant, leopard, sloth bear, gaur (Indian bison), sambar, chital (spotted deer), barking deer, nilgai, the four-horned antelope called chousingha, and the tiny Indian mouse deer. More than 200 species of birds and about 183 species of fish have been recorded here. The river in the gorge is home to the gharial and the mugger crocodile. Rare freshwater turtles also live in the Mahanadi here, and turtles and crocodiles can often be seen basking on sandbanks in the winter sun. Tigers in Satkosia: The tiger population in Satkosia has fallen sharply over the years. In 2018, Satkosia was chosen for India's first inter-state tiger relocation project. A male tiger was brought from Kanha Tiger Reserve and a tigress from Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve, both in Madhya Pradesh. The relocation did not succeed, and protecting the habitat and the prey animals remains the most important task for bringing tigers back.

text: Tikarpada, on the banks of the Mahanadi, is the main eco-tourism centre of Satkosia. It has an interpretation centre, a gharial research and conservation unit, nature trails and camping facilities. Other places known to visitors include Chhotkei, which has a community-run nature camp, and Purunakote, where chital and other animals are often seen. Winter, from November to mid-February, is the most pleasant time to visit. Animals are easier to see in the hot summer months, from mid-February to mid-June, when they gather near water. During the monsoon the Mahanadi can flood, so visitors must follow the advice of forest staff.

section: Angul District and its Forests - About Angul
text: Angul is a district in central Odisha. It became a separate district on 1 April 1993; before that its areas were part of Dhenkanal district. The district covers about 6,232 square kilometres and its headquarters is Angul town, about 150 kilometres from Bhubaneswar. The district is also written as Anugul. The name Angul is linked by local tradition to the word "Anugol". According to legend, the last Khond chief of the area was named Anu, and he was defeated in a struggle called "gol". The Khond, Savara and Gond communities have lived in this region for a very long time. Angul is also an important industrial district of Odisha, known for coal mining, aluminium and steel industries. Because of this, protecting the remaining forests, rivers and wildlife of Angul is especially important. Forest administration: The forests of Angul district are looked after by three forest divisions: Angul Forest Division, Satkosia Wildlife Division and Athamallik Forest Division. Each division is headed by a Divisional Forest Officer, also called the DFO. The forest divisions protect forests and wildlife, raise new plantations, prevent forest fires, reduce conflict between people and elephants, and work with village communities through forest protection committees. The Divisional Forest Officer (DFO) of the Angul Forest Division is Nitish Kumar.

section: Angul District and its Forests - Types of forests
text: Most of the forests in this region are tropical deciduous forests. Deciduous means that the trees shed their leaves in the dry season, mostly between February and April, to save water, and grow fresh leaves before the monsoon. Sal is the most important tree of these forests. Other common trees include Asan, Mahua, Kendu, Bija (Indian kino), Harida, Bahada, Amla, Kusum, Arjun and bamboo. Forests and people: Forests give people many things besides timber. These are called non-timber forest produce, and they include Kendu leaves, Mahua flowers and seeds, Sal leaves and seeds, honey, tamarind, bamboo, broom grass and medicinal plants. Odisha is one of India's largest producers of Kendu leaves, which are used to roll bidis, and leaf collection gives seasonal work to many families living near forests. Forests also protect the soil from erosion, keep streams and rivers flowing, give shelter to wildlife, keep the air clean and store carbon, which helps fight climate change.

section: Elephants of Angul and How to Stay Safe - Elephants in Angul
text: Angul district is part of the range of the Asian elephant in Odisha, and the Satkosia area falls in the Mahanadi Elephant Reserve. Elephants live in herds led by the oldest female, called the matriarch. A herd is usually made of mothers, daughters, aunts and young calves. Adult males often move alone or in small groups. An adult elephant can eat more than 150 kilograms of grass, leaves, bark, bamboo and fruit in a single day, and needs to drink a lot of water. To find enough food, elephants walk long distances along old routes called elephant corridors. When forests are cut or broken up by roads, mines, canals and settlements, elephants sometimes enter villages and crop fields, and conflict with people increases. Elephants are very important for the forest. They spread seeds of many trees through their dung, open up paths in thick forest and dig for water that other animals also use. That is why the elephant is sometimes called a gardener of the forest.

section: Elephants of Angul and How to Stay Safe - How to stay safe near elephants
text: Never go close to an elephant or a herd, and never try to take a selfie with a wild elephant. Do not throw stones, burst crackers, shout or chase elephants. This makes them angry and dangerous. Keep a safe distance, at least a few hundred metres, and leave the elephants a clear path to move away. Avoid walking in the forest or on forest roads in the early morning, late evening and at night, when elephants are most active. If elephants are seen near a village, inform the local forest office or forest staff immediately, and keep away until they arrive. Do not keep country liquor, mahua or ripe fruits stored inside houses in elephant areas, because the smell attracts elephants. Never put up illegal electric fences or live wires. They kill elephants and are a punishable crime. If an elephant charges, do not run in a straight line on open ground; move away quickly, behind large trees or uphill if possible, and drop any bag or cloth that may distract it. Compensation: When people suffer loss of life, injury, or damage to crops or houses because of wild animals, the Government of Odisha provides compensation through the Forest Department. People should report such incidents to the nearest forest office as soon as possible.

section: The Gharial and River Life of the Mahanadi - What is a gharial?
text: The gharial is a crocodile with a very long, thin snout. It is found only in the rivers of the Indian subcontinent. The thin snout is perfect for catching fish, which is almost the only food of an adult gharial, and gharials are generally shy and not a danger to people. Adult males grow a round lump at the tip of the snout called a "ghara", named after an Indian clay pot. That is how the gharial got its name. The gharial is listed as Critically Endangered, which means it faces a very high risk of disappearing from the wild. Its numbers fell because of sand mining, dams, fishing nets in which it gets trapped, and the loss of the sandbanks it needs for nesting and basking. Gharials in Satkosia: The Mahanadi River in the Satkosia Gorge is the natural home of gharials in Odisha. A gharial research and conservation unit works at Tikarpada. Gharial eggs are collected and hatched safely, and the young are reared until they are big enough, and then released back into the Mahanadi. This method is called "rear and release".

section: The Gharial and River Life of the Mahanadi - The mugger crocodile
text: The mugger, or marsh crocodile, also lives in the Mahanadi. It has a broad, strong snout and eats fish, birds and mammals. Unlike the gharial, a mugger can be dangerous to people and cattle, so visitors must never go into the water or close to the river bank where muggers are seen. Freshwater turtles and fish: Rare freshwater turtles, including softshell turtles, live in the Mahanadi in Satkosia. Turtles help keep rivers clean by eating dead fish and plants. About 183 species of fish have been recorded in the reserve. How you can help river life: Do not throw plastic or waste into rivers. Do not buy turtle meat or turtle shells; hunting and trading turtles is a crime. Report illegal fishing with poison or explosives, and illegal sand mining, to the forest department.

section: Common Trees and Birds of the Angul Forests - Sal
text: Sal (Shorea robusta) is the most important tree of the forests of Odisha. It is a tall tree with hard, strong wood. Sal leaves are stitched together to make leaf plates and cups, which are a natural replacement for plastic plates. Sal seeds are collected by forest communities and the seed oil has many uses. Sal trees drop many of their leaves in the dry season and grow new leaves quickly, so the forest stays green for most of the year. Mahua: Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) is a large tree loved by forest communities. Its sweet, juicy flowers fall in the early summer and are collected in the morning to be eaten, dried and sold. Its seeds give an oil used for cooking and lighting. Many animals, including bears, deer and birds, also eat mahua flowers. Kendu: Kendu (Diospyros melanoxylon) is a small tree whose leaves are used to roll bidis. It gives seasonal income to many families. Its fruit is eaten by people, birds and animals.

section: Common Trees and Birds of the Angul Forests - Other useful trees
text: Harida, Bahada and Amla are three trees whose fruits are used together in the traditional medicine called Triphala. Arjun trees grow along rivers and streams and their bark is used in traditional medicine. Bija, also called Indian kino, gives a red gum. Asan trees are used to rear tasar silkworms. Bamboo grows fast and is used for building, baskets and many crafts. Odisha state symbols: The state animal of Odisha is the Sambar deer. The state bird of Odisha is the Indian roller, also called the blue jay, known for its brilliant blue wings in flight. The state tree is the Ashwatha, or peepal, and the state flower is the Ashoka. Birds of the forest: More than 200 species of birds have been recorded in the Satkosia area. Birds commonly seen in these forests include the Indian peafowl, red junglefowl, Indian grey hornbill, Indian roller, various owls, kingfishers along rivers, and birds of prey such as the crested serpent eagle. River birds like cormorants, egrets and herons are seen along the Mahanadi. Many migratory birds visit the rivers and wetlands in winter. Why birds matter: Birds spread seeds, pollinate flowers and eat insects that can harm crops. Owls and birds of prey control rats in fields. A forest with many kinds of birds is usually a healthy forest.

section: Forest Fire Prevention and Rules for Visitors - Forest fires
text: Most forest fires in Odisha happen in the dry season, from about February to June, when fallen leaves on the forest floor become dry. Almost all forest fires are caused by people, for example by burning leaves to collect mahua flowers easily, throwing away burning bidis or matchsticks, or fires spreading from fields. Forest fires kill small animals, birds' eggs and young plants, damage the soil and fill the air with smoke. How to prevent forest fires: Never throw a lit bidi, cigarette or matchstick in or near a forest. Do not light fires inside the forest. Use only the fire places allowed by forest staff at camps. When collecting mahua flowers, sweep the ground clean instead of burning the leaves. If you see a forest fire, inform the nearest forest office, the forest protection committee of your village, or forest staff immediately.

section: Forest Fire Prevention and Rules for Visitors - Rules for visitors in forests and protected areas
text: Enter protected areas only through the official gates and with the required permits, and only during the permitted hours. Stay on the marked roads and trails, and always follow the instructions of forest staff and guides. Do not feed, tease or disturb wild animals, and keep a safe distance from them. Keep silence in the forest. Loud music, horns and shouting disturb animals. Do not carry plastic, and carry all your waste back with you. Do not pluck plants or flowers, and do not collect anything from the forest. Hunting, carrying weapons, and harming any wild animal are serious crimes under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. Do not drink alcohol in protected areas. Be a friend of the forest: Plant trees and look after them. Save paper and water. Say no to plastic. Never buy products made from wild animals, such as skins, ivory, horns or turtle shells. Tell others what you learnt about forests and wildlife today.
